Each question carries 20 marks. Verify that this booklet contains six questions, no questions are repeated and there are no blank pages. Inform the invigilator in case this booklet contains less than six questions, questions are repeated or there are blank pages so that the booklet should be changed. Blank spaces in this question booklet may be used for rough work. In calculations you are advised to show all the steps in your working, giving your answer at each stage. All necessary working must be shown. No marks will be awarded for answers without brief statements showing how the answers have been obtained. Noiseless calculators may be used.

**Useful data:** $R = 8.314\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}$ or $0.082\ \mathrm{atm\,dm^{3}\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}$. One atmosphere (1 atm) = 1 Pa = $1.01\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}$ (as printed). Relative atomic masses (RAM): C = 12.0, O = 16.0, S = 32.0, H = 1.0, Cl = 35.5.

The paper has three sections: Section A - Physical and General Chemistry (questions 1 and 2); Section B - Inorganic Chemistry (questions 3 and 4); Section C - Organic Chemistry (questions 5 and 6). All six questions are compulsory.

questions.enonce_markdown:
The elements in group I and II of the periodic table are called s-block elements.

(i) Why are they called s-block elements?

(ii) Write equations to show the effect of heat on sodium carbonate, $\mathrm{Na_2CO_3}$ and calcium carbonate, $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$.

Sodium carbonate:

Calcium carbonate: *[3 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** They are called **s-block elements** because the **outermost (valence) electrons occupy an $s$ subshell**: the last electron added to the atom enters an $s$ orbital (general configuration $ns^1$ for Group I and $ns^2$ for Group II).

**(ii) Effect of heat.**

**Sodium carbonate:** it is **thermally stable** and **does not decompose** at the temperature of a Bunsen burner: $\mathrm{Na_2CO_3(s)} \xrightarrow{\text{heat}}$ no reaction (it only melts at about $850^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$). The large $\mathrm{Na^+}$ ion has a low charge density and polarises the carbonate ion very little.

**Calcium carbonate:** it **decomposes** on strong heating to calcium oxide and carbon dioxide:

$\mathrm{CaCO_3(s)} \xrightarrow{\text{heat}} \mathrm{CaO(s)} + \mathrm{CO_2(g)}$

The smaller, doubly charged $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$ ion has a higher charge density and polarises the carbonate ion enough to weaken a C-O bond and cause decomposition.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Lithium and magnesium are said to show a diagonal relationship.

(i) Give 2 reasons why these elements show this relationship.

(ii) With the help of chemical equations, use the nitrate of the elements to show the relationship *[4 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Two reasons.**

1. **Similar charge density (charge-to-radius ratio), hence similar polarising power:** $\mathrm{Li^+}$ (radius about $0.076\ \mathrm{nm}$, charge $+1$) and $\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}$ (radius about $0.072\ \mathrm{nm}$, charge $+2$) have similar ionic radii, and going down a group (radius up) and to the right (charge up) roughly cancel.
2. **Similar electronegativities** (Li $1.0$, Mg $1.2$) and similar atomic radii (about $0.152\ \mathrm{nm}$ and $0.160\ \mathrm{nm}$), so their compounds have a similar degree of covalent character.

**(ii) Nitrates.** The nitrates of lithium and magnesium **both decompose on heating to the oxide, nitrogen dioxide and oxygen**, unlike the nitrates of the other Group I metals, which only give the nitrite and oxygen:

$4\mathrm{LiNO_3(s)} \xrightarrow{\text{heat}} 2\mathrm{Li_2O(s)} + 4\mathrm{NO_2(g)} + \mathrm{O_2(g)}$

$2\mathrm{Mg(NO_3)_2(s)} \xrightarrow{\text{heat}} 2\mathrm{MgO(s)} + 4\mathrm{NO_2(g)} + \mathrm{O_2(g)}$

For comparison: $2\mathrm{NaNO_3(s)} \xrightarrow{\text{heat}} 2\mathrm{NaNO_2(s)} + \mathrm{O_2(g)}$.

Atom check: Li 4 = 4, N 4 = 4, O $12 = 2 + 8 + 2$; Mg 2 = 2, N 4 = 4, O $12 = 2 + 8 + 2$.

questions.enonce_markdown:
This question concerns the halogens and hydrogen halides

(i) Complete the table below by giving the formula and name of compounds of chlorine with the oxidation states indicated.

| Oxidation state | Formula | Name of compound |
|---|---|---|
| +5 | | |
| +7 | | |

(ii) Write a balanced equation for the reaction of chlorine with hot concentrated potassium hydroxide solution.

(iii) What is the type of reaction taking place in c(ii) above

(iv) Hydrogen chloride can be prepared by treating sodium chloride with concentrated sulphuric acid. Why is this method not suitable for the preparation of hydrogen bromide?

(v) Which acid can be used to obtain HBr from sodium bromide? *[7 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Compounds of chlorine.**

| Oxidation state | Formula | Name of compound |
|---|---|---|
| +5 | $\mathrm{KClO_3}$ (contains $\mathrm{ClO_3^-}$; or $\mathrm{HClO_3}$) | potassium chlorate(V) (chloric(V) acid for $\mathrm{HClO_3}$) |
| +7 | $\mathrm{KClO_4}$ (contains $\mathrm{ClO_4^-}$; or $\mathrm{HClO_4}$) | potassium chlorate(VII), potassium perchlorate (chloric(VII) acid for $\mathrm{HClO_4}$) |

Check: $\mathrm{ClO_3^-}$: $x + 3(-2) = -1$ gives $x = +5$; $\mathrm{ClO_4^-}$: $x + 4(-2) = -1$ gives $x = +7$.

**(ii) Equation.**

$3\mathrm{Cl_2(g)} + 6\mathrm{KOH(aq)} \rightarrow 5\mathrm{KCl(aq)} + \mathrm{KClO_3(aq)} + 3\mathrm{H_2O(l)}$

Atom check: Cl $6 = 5 + 1$; K $6 = 5 + 1$; O $6 = 3 + 3$; H $6 = 6$.

**(iii) Type of reaction: disproportionation** (a redox reaction in which the same element is simultaneously oxidised and reduced): chlorine goes from $0$ to $-1$ in $\mathrm{KCl}$ (reduced) and from $0$ to $+5$ in $\mathrm{KClO_3}$ (oxidised).

**(iv) Why not for HBr.** Concentrated sulphuric acid is an **oxidising agent**. $\mathrm{HBr}$ (bromide ion) is a **stronger reducing agent than $\mathrm{HCl}$**, so as soon as it forms it is **oxidised to bromine** (orange-brown fumes), while the sulphuric acid is reduced to sulphur dioxide: $2\mathrm{HBr} + \mathrm{H_2SO_4} \rightarrow \mathrm{Br_2} + \mathrm{SO_2} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}$. The product is therefore contaminated with $\mathrm{Br_2}$ and $\mathrm{SO_2}$ (chloride is too weak a reducing agent to be oxidised).

**(v) Acid to use:** **concentrated phosphoric(V) acid, $\mathrm{H_3PO_4}$** (a non-oxidising acid): $\mathrm{NaBr} + \mathrm{H_3PO_4} \rightarrow \mathrm{NaH_2PO_4} + \mathrm{HBr}$.

questions.enonce_markdown:
The elements in group IV of the periodic table are Carbon, Silicon, Germanium, Tin and Lead.

(i) State the trend in the relative stability of the oxidation states for the elements.

(ii) Give the general formula of the tetrachlorides of the group IV elements.

(iii) Write the equations of the reactions of the tetrachloride of carbon and silicon with water.

A: carbon tetrachloride:

B: Silicon tetrachloride:

(iv) Which of these elements exhibits extensive catenation? *[6 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Trend in the stability of the oxidation states.** Going **down** the group, the **$+4$ state becomes less stable and the $+2$ state more stable** (the **inert pair effect**: the $ns^2$ electrons become increasingly reluctant to take part in bonding). Carbon and silicon are almost always $+4$; for germanium $+4$ is still more stable than $+2$; for tin $+2$ and $+4$ have similar stability ($\mathrm{Sn^{2+}}$ is a mild reducing agent); for lead $+2$ is the more stable state and $\mathrm{Pb(IV)}$ compounds such as $\mathrm{PbO_2}$ are strong oxidising agents.

**(ii) General formula of the tetrachlorides:** $\mathrm{XCl_4}$ (where X = C, Si, Ge, Sn or Pb).

**(iii) Reactions with water.**

**A: carbon tetrachloride:** it is **not hydrolysed**; $\mathrm{CCl_4} + \mathrm{H_2O} \rightarrow$ **no reaction**. (Carbon has no vacant low-energy d orbitals to accept a lone pair from water, and the small carbon atom is shielded by four large chlorine atoms.)

**B: Silicon tetrachloride:** it is **hydrolysed rapidly**, giving white fumes of hydrogen chloride and a white solid of silicon dioxide (hydrated):

$\mathrm{SiCl_4(l)} + 2\mathrm{H_2O(l)} \rightarrow \mathrm{SiO_2(s)} + 4\mathrm{HCl(g)}$

(or $\mathrm{SiCl_4} + 4\mathrm{H_2O} \rightarrow \mathrm{Si(OH)_4} + 4\mathrm{HCl}$). Silicon can use its vacant $3d$ orbitals to accept lone pairs from water.

**(iv) Catenation:** **carbon** shows extensive catenation (the ability to form long chains and rings of its own atoms), because the **$\mathrm{C{-}C}$ bond is very strong** (about $346\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$, compared with about $222\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ for $\mathrm{Si{-}Si}$).
